note: The same eight-part structure as the Korean grammar file. The points themselves have nothing in common with Korean's — that is the whole reason each language owns its own curriculum.

points.name: です
points.simple: Put です after a noun to say something is that thing. Unlike Korean's 이에요/예요, there is only one form — nothing depends on the sound before it.
points.technical: The polite copula. Its plain form is だ. Attaches to nouns and na-adjectives; with i-adjectives it adds politeness only, since the adjective is already the predicate.

examples.note: na-adjective — です does the work.
i-adjective — です is politeness only, not a copula.

mistakes.why: i-adjectives never take だ.
だ and です are the same word at different politeness levels — never both.
Japanese marks questions with か, so the question mark is optional and often omitted.

questions.why: A noun takes です directly.

prompts.situation: Someone asks what you do. You're a student.

points.name: は (topic)
points.simple: は puts something on the table and says 'right, let's talk about this'. It is written は but read wa. It often carries a quiet contrast — 私は says 'as for me, whatever anyone else does'.
points.technical: The topic marker. Marks known information, contrast or generic statements. Read /wa/ — a historical spelling preserved for the particle only.

examples.why: Implies other days may not be.

examples.target: コーヒーは好きですが、お茶は嫌いです。
examples.english: I like coffee but not tea.

mistakes.wrong: Reading は as 'ha' in 私は
mistakes.why: As a particle it is always read wa.
Question words take が, never は — you cannot make a topic of something unknown.

prompts.situation: Say that today specifically is hot.

points.name: が (subject)
points.simple: が points at something new. If it answers 'who?' or 'what?', or if it has just walked into the conversation, it takes が.
points.technical: The subject marker. Marks new or focused information, and is obligatory in subordinate clauses where は cannot occur. Also used with 好き, 嫌い, 上手, ある, いる and 分かる.

examples.why: 好き is an adjective, so the liked thing is the subject.

mistakes.why: 好き is a na-adjective, not a verb. There is no object.
分かる also takes が.

points.name: を (object)
points.simple: を marks what the action happens to. Eat what? Read what? That gets を. It is the only place this character appears in modern Japanese, and it is pronounced exactly like お.
points.technical: The accusative marker. Also marks the path traversed with motion verbs: 公園を歩く.

mistakes.why: 行く takes a destination with に, not an object.
会う takes に. Korean does the opposite — 친구를 만나요 — so Korean speakers get this one wrong often.
乗る takes に.

prompts: Say three things you did today.

prompts.situation: Tell someone you're reading a book.

points.name: に and で
points.meaning: at, to, in, by means of
points.simple: に is a pin stuck in a place or a time. で is a stage the action happens on. If you could film someone doing the verb there, use で.
points.technical: に marks destination, point in time, indirect object, and location of existence with いる/ある. で marks the location of a dynamic activity and the instrument or means.

mistakes.why: いる and ある take に without exception.
今日, 明日, 昨日 and 今 never take に.

prompts: どこで働いていますか。

points.name: ます form
points.simple: The form you will use most. Ichidan verbs drop る and add ます. Godan verbs shift their last kana into the i-column and add ます: 書く becomes 書きます.
points.technical: The polite non-past. Covers both present and future — Japanese does not distinguish them. Negative ません, past ました, past negative ませんでした.
points.structure: ichidan: drop る + ます  |  godan: i-column + ます

mistakes.why: 食べる is ichidan: る simply drops.
帰る looks ichidan but is godan.
ます attaches to the i-column stem, not the dictionary form.

prompts: Say five things you do every day.

points.name: て form
points.simple: The single most useful form in Japanese. On its own it joins clauses; with something attached it makes requests, permission, prohibition and the progressive. Learn the sound changes and dozens of structures open up at once.
points.technical: The gerundive form, produced by 音便 (euphonic change). The ending depends on the dictionary-final kana, and 行く is the one exception.
points.structure: う/つ/る → って   ぬ/ぶ/む → んで   く → いて   ぐ → いで   す → して   ichidan: る → て

examples.target: ちょっと待ってください。

mistakes.why: 行く is the one godan く verb that goes って.
む goes to んで, not みて.
Ichidan verbs never take っ.

prompts.situation: Ask someone to wait a moment.
prompts.target: ちょっと待ってください。

points.name: ない form
points.simple: Godan verbs shift into the a-column and add ない. Ichidan verbs drop る and add ない. One trap: verbs ending in う go to わ, not あ.
points.technical: The plain negative. ある is suppletive — its negative is ない, never あらない.
points.structure: godan: a-column + ない  |  ichidan: drop る + ない

examples.note: う goes to わ, not あ.

mistakes.why: The う row's a-form is わ. Historical, and it applies to every う verb.
ある's negative is a separate word.

points.name: Counters
points.simple: You cannot just say 'three books' in Japanese. The number needs a counter word attached, and which counter depends on the shape of the thing. When you do not know, つ works for almost anything up to ten.
points.technical: Numeral classifiers. Sino-Japanese numerals combine with most counters; native numerals survive in つ, 人 (partly) and a few others. Several counters trigger sound changes: 本 → ほん/ぼん/ぽん.

examples.target: ビールを二本ください。
りんごを三つください。

examples.english: The two of us are going.
examples.note: 人 for people; two is irregular.

mistakes.wrong: 三本 read さんほん
mistakes.why: 本 shifts between ほん, ぼん and ぽん. Learn the set as a unit.
One and two people are irregular: ひとり and ふたり.

mistakes.wrong: 二十歳 read にじゅっさい
mistakes.why: Twenty years old has its own word.

prompts.target: ビールを二本ください。

points.name: Godan versus ichidan
points.simple: Every Japanese verb is one of two types, plus two irregulars. Ichidan verbs are easy — drop る, attach anything. Godan verbs shift their last kana up and down a column. Which type a verb is decides every single form, so it is worth getting right early.
points.technical: Ichidan (一段) verbs have an invariant stem; godan (五段) verbs alternate across the five vowel grades of the stem-final consonant row. する and 来る are suppletive.
points.structure: ends in る with i/e before it → usually ichidan; everything else → godan

examples.target: 食べる → 食べます / 食べない / 食べて
取る → 取ります / 取らない / 取って
examples.english: godan — る moves through り, ら, っ

mistakes.why: 帰る is godan despite the え before る.
見る is ichidan, but the kanji hides the い — you have to know this one.

prompts: Say the ます form of five verbs.

prompts.situation: Say you go home at six.
